The company's response will likely influence consumer trust in future Legion Go purchases and in Lenovo's broader gaming brand.

title: Zillow and Redfin settle FTC antitrust case over their rental listings partnership
summary: The FTC and Zillow have announced a settlement that ends the case alleging that a 2025 "partnership" between Zillow and Redfin violated antitrust laws. The FTC had alleged Zillow agreed to pay Redfin to syndicate its listings, while Redfin would end its own advertising contracts…
whatHappening: The FTC and Zillow have reached a settlement ending an antitrust case that challenged a 2025 partnership between Zillow and Redfin. The deal allegedly involved Zillow paying Redfin to syndicate listings while Redfin would discontinue its own advertising contracts—a structure the FTC argued violated antitrust law.
whoInvolved: Zillow Group, Inc., a real-estate marketplace company founded in 2006 by former Microsoft executives including Rich Barton and Lloyd Frink, and Redfin, a real estate services subsidiary of Rocket Companies that operates in the U.S. and Canada. The Federal Trade Commission brought the case alleging anticompetitive conduct.
whyMatters: The settlement clarifies limits on how competing real-estate platforms can structure deals involving listing syndication and advertising exclusivity. The outcome will influence future partnerships in the fragmented real-estate digital marketplace and may reshape how platforms balance competitive reach with partnership arrangements.
articleBody:
The Federal Trade Commission has reached a settlement with Zillow in a case alleging that a proposed partnership between Zillow and Redfin would have violated antitrust laws. According to The Verge, the FTC had challenged the arrangement on grounds that it would have reduced competition in the rental listings market through an agreement in which Zillow would pay Redfin to syndicate its listings in exchange for Redfin ending its own advertising contracts.

Zillow Group, Inc., founded in 2006 by former Microsoft executives Rich Barton and Lloyd Frink—who previously founded the travel platform Expedia—operates one of the largest real-estate marketplaces in the United States. Redfin, a subsidiary of Rocket Companies, provides real estate agent services for buying, selling, and renting homes across the U.S. and Canada. The two companies had announced their partnership for 2025, which would have created a significant realignment in how listings are distributed and promoted across competing platforms.

The FTC's challenge focused on the structure of the deal: by paying Redfin to syndicate listings rather than allowing Redfin to independently decide whether to advertise competing inventory, the arrangement would have reduced Redfin's incentive to compete for advertising placements. This, the FTC argued, would ultimately harm consumers by limiting competitive choices in how rental properties are advertised and discovered online.

The settlement resolves the case without determining whether the partnership would have actually violated antitrust law, and the terms of the settlement remain subject to the specifics outlined in the agreement. Such settlements typically require companies to unwind the challenged arrangement or to agree to modified terms that address the FTC's competitive concerns.

The case reflects ongoing regulatory scrutiny of major technology platforms in the real-estate sector, where listing syndication and advertising placement have become critical competitive battlegrounds. As Zillow and Redfin both operate major platforms with significant market presence, decisions about how they distribute and promote listings ripple across the entire industry, affecting smaller brokers, agents, and ultimately consumers searching for homes.

title: The cat-and-mouse game over 3D-printed guns has begun
summary: The creator of the world's first 3D-printed gun claims he's developed a way to thwart government-mandated software meant to block 3D printers from making firearms. It's an opening volley in what's shaping up to be an evolving battle between regulators trying to stem the tide of…
whatHappening: The creator of the first 3D-printed gun claims to have developed a method to bypass government-mandated software designed to prevent 3D printers from manufacturing firearms. This move opens a new front in an escalating regulatory battle between law enforcement and those pushing to democratize gun manufacturing through digital design.
whoInvolved: Cody Wilson, founder of Defense Distributed, is at the center of this dispute. Wilson is a gun rights activist and crypto-anarchist whose organization publishes open-source firearm designs as CAD files for 3D printing and CNC milling. Defense Distributed gained international attention in 2013 when it released plans for the Liberator, the first widely available functioning 3D-printed pistol.
whyMatters: This escalation threatens to undermine regulatory efforts to control homemade firearm production and distribution. If Wilson's workaround proves viable and spreads, it could render software-based restrictions ineffective, forcing regulators into a perpetual cycle of technological cat-and-mouse with no clear endpoint. The outcome will likely shape how governments approach digital manufacturing oversight for years to come.
articleBody:
The battle over 3D-printed firearms is entering a new phase. According to The Verge, the creator of the world's first 3D-printed gun now claims to have developed a method to circumvent government-mandated software designed to block 3D printers from producing firearms. This move represents an opening salvo in what appears to be an escalating conflict between regulatory authorities seeking to stem the proliferation of homemade weapons and advocates pushing to democratize firearm manufacturing through digital design.

Cody Wilson, the founder of Defense Distributed, has been at the forefront of this movement since 2013, when his organization published plans for the Liberator—the first widely available functioning 3D-printed pistol. Defense Distributed operates as an open-source hardware and software organization, developing digital schematics for firearms as CAD files available for download and use in 3D printing or CNC milling applications. Wilson, a gun rights activist and crypto-anarchist, has framed the work as supporting the popular production of homemade firearms, positioning it as a matter of democratic access to manufacturing capability.

Governments around the world have moved to restrict access to these designs and manufacturing capabilities. In response to the proliferation of 3D-printed gun plans, regulators have pursued software-based solutions intended to prevent 3D printers from executing files containing firearm components. These mandates represent a technological approach to a novel problem: how to control what can be manufactured when the tools themselves are becoming more widely available and harder to regulate.

Wilson's claimed breakthrough in circumventing this software represents a fundamental challenge to that regulatory strategy. If his method proves effective and becomes widely known, it could render software locks largely obsolete, forcing governments back to the drawing board. The implications extend beyond firearms themselves—the underlying conflict reflects broader tensions over digital manufacturing, open-source design, and the extent to which governments can control what gets made in an era of increasingly accessible production technology.

The stakes are particularly high because this is not a static battle but an evolving one. Each regulatory innovation will likely be met with countermeasures, creating a dynamic cycle in which neither side can claim permanent victory. Unlike traditional gun regulation, which relies on supply chains and physical manufacturing infrastructure, digital firearm design operates at the speed of software development and information distribution.

title: Raspberry Pi shares its official tutorial for making a cyberdeck
summary: Raspberry Pi's head of social, Ashley Whittaker, acknowledged the cyberdeck trend today, saying "we haven't been able to get away from cyberdecks this year." Tiny portable computers made out of things like purses, jewelry boxes, and other thrifted or recycled parts have gone…
whatHappening: Raspberry Pi has officially embraced the cyberdeck trend by releasing a tutorial for building one, acknowledging that these custom portable computers have become impossible to ignore in the maker community. The company's head of social media noted that cyberdecks have dominated conversations around the platform throughout the year.
whoInvolved: Raspberry Pi, a UK-based manufacturer of small single-board computers (SBCs) originally developed by the Raspberry Pi Foundation in collaboration with Broadcom, is taking an official stance on the cyberdeck movement. Ashley Whittaker, Raspberry Pi's head of social, is the company representative quoted on the trend.
whyMatters: By releasing an official cyberdeck tutorial, Raspberry Pi is legitimizing a grassroots maker movement while capitalizing on growing demand for customizable portable computing devices. This move signals that niche hardware trends can transition into mainstream recognition when they reach critical mass in the enthusiast community.
articleBody:
Raspberry Pi, the UK-based manufacturer of single-board computers, has officially weighed in on one of this year's biggest maker trends: cyberdecks. According to The Verge, Ashley Whittaker, Raspberry Pi's head of social, acknowledged the cyberdeck phenomenon by saying the company "hasn't been able to get away from cyberdecks this year."

A cyberdeck is a custom-built, portable personal computer typically designed for individualized purposes and featuring a cyberpunk aesthetic. These devices are individually crafted by makers using laptop motherboards or single-board computers like Raspberry Pis, and they incorporate displays, keyboards, and housings made from thrifted or recycled materials such as purses, jewelry boxes, and other repurposed objects. The aesthetic appeals to a growing community of DIY computer enthusiasts who view computing hardware as a canvas for creative expression.

Raspberry Pi's decision to publish an official tutorial represents a significant shift in how the company engages with grassroots maker culture. By providing guidance on cyberdeck construction, the company is not simply acknowledging the trend—it is actively participating in and legitimizing it. This move transforms cyberdecks from an underground niche hobby into something with corporate backing and institutional support.

The timing reflects the rapid acceleration of the cyberdeck movement within the maker community. What began as scattered individual projects by hobbyists has evolved into a recognizable subculture with its own aesthetics, communities, and shared design principles. Raspberry Pi's involvement suggests the trend has reached a tipping point where ignoring it was no longer feasible for a company whose products are at the core of many of these builds.

For Raspberry Pi Holdings, the company's commercial entity, this tutorial represents both a marketing opportunity and a genuine engagement with its user base. Single-board computers have always been positioned as educational and hackable devices, and cyberdecks embody exactly that spirit—transforming commodity hardware into something personalized and unique. By providing official guidance, Raspberry Pi strengthens its brand identity as a platform for creative makers rather than just a component supplier.

title: Two great new repairable gadgets
summary: Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 141, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you're new here, welcome, I'm newish here too, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.) This week, I've been getting back into the Installer…
whatHappening: The Verge's Installer newsletter has highlighted two new gadgets that prioritize repairability, a growing consumer concern. The featured products represent a shift toward devices designed to be fixed rather than replaced.
whoInvolved: The Verge, a technology and culture publication, curates consumer gadget recommendations through its Installer newsletter series. The newsletter, now in its 141st edition, serves as a guide to notable technology products and consumer goods.
whyMatters: The spotlight on repairable gadgets reflects increasing consumer demand for sustainable technology and reduced electronic waste. As manufacturers face pressure to extend product lifecycles, repairability has become a competitive differentiator in the consumer electronics market, affecting both environmental impact and long-term ownership costs.
articleBody:
Consumer electronics have long followed a pattern of planned obsolescence, with manufacturers designing products meant to be discarded rather than repaired. But a new wave of gadgets is challenging that approach by prioritizing durability and user-friendly fixes. According to The Verge, this week's Installer newsletter features two standout products that exemplify this shift toward repairability.

The move toward repairable gadgets addresses a mounting problem: electronic waste. When devices cannot be easily serviced or upgraded, consumers face the choice of either living with degraded performance or purchasing replacements entirely. This cycle has contributed to millions of tons of e-waste annually, filled with valuable materials and toxic components. By designing products that users can repair themselves or service through accessible channels, manufacturers can significantly extend the useful life of their goods.

The Installer series has built its reputation on identifying products that matter to consumers seeking quality and thoughtful design. The newsletter's 141st edition continues this tradition while reflecting broader market changes. Tech companies increasingly recognize that repairability appeals to environmentally conscious consumers and can reduce support costs through customer self-service repairs. Right-to-repair movements have also pressured manufacturers to make spare parts and repair documentation more accessible.

These two featured gadgets represent different product categories, yet share a common philosophy: devices should be serviceable throughout their lifespan. Whether through modular designs that allow component swaps, easily replaceable batteries, or straightforward access to internal parts, repairable products reduce the barrier between a malfunctioning device and a working one. This approach benefits consumers economically while supporting sustainability goals.

As consumer awareness of e-waste and product lifecycles grows, repairability is becoming a key purchasing criterion alongside traditional factors like performance and price. The gadgets highlighted in this week's Installer stand as evidence that the market is responding to these shifting priorities, with manufacturers investing in designs that prove devices can be both innovative and lasting.

title: GTA VI: all the news on Rockstar’s next entry in the Grand Theft Auto series
summary: It’s been over a decade and two console generations since GTA V came out, and its sequel is still a work in progress. GTA VI has faced multiple delays, with developer Rockstar Games bumping back its predicted release date twice, first to May 26th, 2026, then again to November…
whatHappening: Grand Theft Auto VI, the long-awaited sequel to Rockstar Games' flagship franchise, has been delayed again—this time to November 2026. The game, which has faced multiple pushbacks over more than a decade of development, remains a work in progress at the studio.
whoInvolved: Rockstar Games, the American video game publisher based in New York City and a subsidiary of Take-Two Interactive, is developing GTA VI through its British development house Rockstar North. The studio is led by president Sam Houser, one of the founding brothers who has overseen the Grand Theft Auto series since its creation.
whyMatters: GTA VI is one of the most anticipated releases in gaming, and the repeated delays signal ongoing challenges in developing a sequel to one of the best-selling franchises in entertainment history. The extended timeline affects not only gamers awaiting the game, but also Rockstar Games' parent company Take-Two Interactive and the broader industry's release schedule.
articleBody:
Rockstar Games has pushed back the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI once again, with the publisher now targeting November 2026 as the new release date. According to The Verge, the game has faced multiple delays, with developer Rockstar Games initially bumping back its predicted release to May 26th, 2026, before delaying it further to the fall. The extended development timeline underscores the complexity of creating a new mainline entry in one of gaming's most successful franchises.

More than a decade has passed since Grand Theft Auto V's release, and two full console generations have come and gone. The original GTA V launched in 2013 and went on to become a cultural phenomenon, generating billions in revenue and remaining commercially viable through online updates and re-releases. That longevity has set an extraordinarily high bar for its successor, placing significant pressure on Rockstar to deliver a game that justifies the wait.

Rockstar Games, established in December 1998 as a subsidiary of Take-Two Interactive, has built its reputation on sprawling open-world games that push technical and creative boundaries. The company was founded by industry veterans including brothers Dan and Sam Houser, who later oversaw development of the Grand Theft Auto series. The franchise itself, created by David Jones and Mike Dailly, has been developed under the oversight of the Houser brothers alongside Leslie Benzies and Aaron Garbut, with Rockstar North handling primary development duties.

The repeated delays reflect the scale of ambition behind GTA VI. Creating a new mainline Grand Theft Auto game requires not only advanced technical work across multiple platforms, but also the design and implementation of sprawling virtual worlds filled with detailed missions, characters, and systems. The gap since GTA V's release means players and industry observers have built substantial expectations, raising the stakes for a release that must justify over a decade of anticipation.

With November 2026 now targeted, Rockstar Games and its parent company Take-Two Interactive have signaled their commitment to releasing a finished product rather than rushing the game to market. The decision reflects a calculated approach: missing another deadline would be far more damaging than the delays themselves have proven to be.

title: Grand Theft Auto VI exists in its own universe

whatHappening: Grand Theft Auto VI is being developed as a self-contained universe distinct from previous entries in the franchise. The upcoming game, set in the fictional state of Leonida and featuring the criminal duo Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, marks a deliberate creative shift for Rockstar Games.
whoInvolved: Rockstar Games, the New York City-based video game publisher and subsidiary of Take-Two Interactive, is developing the title. The studio, headed by president Sam Houser, has been a dominant force in open-world game design since its 1998 founding.
whyMatters: This universe-building approach suggests Rockstar is rethinking how it connects or separates its flagship franchise entries, potentially influencing how players experience the game's narrative and world. The decision reflects broader industry trends toward standalone storytelling within established franchises and could shape expectations for how GTA VI relates to its predecessor, 2013's Grand Theft Auto V.
articleBody:
Rockstar Games is crafting Grand Theft Auto VI as its own distinct universe, a creative decision that underscores the studio's approach to the eighth main entry in its iconic franchise. The game, set within the fictional US state of Leonida—a Florida-inspired setting—centers on the story of Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, a romantic criminal duo navigating an open world that includes the Miami-inspired Vice City. According to The Verge, this universe-building framework represents a notable departure in how Rockstar is positioning the game within the broader Grand Theft Auto canon.

The decision to establish GTA VI in its own universe comes as Rockstar Games prepares for one of the most anticipated releases in the video game industry. As the sixteenth entry overall in the franchise, GTA VI follows a thirteen-year gap since Grand Theft Auto V's 2013 debut. That predecessor became a cultural phenomenon and one of the best-selling games of all time, setting an extraordinarily high bar for its successor. By anchoring GTA VI in a self-contained narrative world, Rockstar appears to be signaling that players should approach this entry on its own terms rather than as a direct continuation of the previous game's storyline and setting.

This creative choice has implications for how the game will be received and experienced by both longtime fans and newcomers. A dedicated universe allows Rockstar to establish fresh storytelling without being constrained by the narrative baggage of Grand Theft Auto V, while still maintaining the core gameplay mechanics and open-world design that define the franchise. The focus on the romantic criminal narrative of Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval suggests the studio is exploring character-driven storytelling as a central pillar of the experience.

For Rockstar Games, headed by president Sam Houser since the studio's 1998 founding, the approach reflects a matured understanding of franchise management in an era where players increasingly expect meaningful narrative depth from AAA experiences. The company's deliberate framing of GTA VI as its own universe may also serve a practical purpose: it allows the studio to innovate on the formula without having to reconcile continuity with earlier games or address why certain characters or locations may have changed.

As development continues, the universe-building framework will likely influence discussions around GTA VI's place in gaming history and whether it can match the unprecedented commercial and cultural success of its predecessor.
